issues.description: Loop invariant for the three-state machine is not stated anywhere in the code.
issues.detail: The DFS-with-explicit-stack maintains an invariant: every node on the stack is either `unsorted` (not yet entered) or `walking` (children pushed, awaiting post-visit). Collapsing `working`/`walking` into one state makes this invariant tighter, but the comment never says so. A reader cannot verify correctness without reconstructing it. Add a one-paragraph literate comment stating the invariant and the meaning of each state.

issues.description: Cycle detection via push() relies on a state that no longer distinguishes "on stack" from "fully walked."
issues.detail: Previously `working` meant "on the stack, children being processed" and `sorted` meant "emitted." Now `walking` covers the on-stack case, but a node is only marked `sorted` after yield. Between popping and yielding the node still appears `walking` to push(). Verify push()'s back-edge handling still terminates and reports cycles correctly; the invariant change deserves an audit comment.

issues.description: Deferred clear(s.stack) over the full backing array is wasted work since len is then reset to 0.
issues.detail: `clear(s.stack)` zeroes every element up to len, then `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` discards them logically. For pointer/interface Node types this is necessary to drop GC references; for value types it is pure overhead. Worth a one-line comment explaining the GC motivation, or condition on Node kind. Asymptotically O(n) cleanup on every Sort call regardless.

issues.description: Typos in the new comment undermine the literate-programming standard the rest of the file holds.
issues.detail: "visisted" and "if its" (should be "it's") appear in the new explanatory comment. The original comment was carefully written (note the diaeresis on "reëntrantly"); this regression in prose quality is small but worth fixing in a file that clearly cares about its reader.

issues.description: Removal of `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` (a no-op) is correct but the replacement leaves first-call behavior implicit.
issues.detail: The old line `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` did nothing meaningful (full reslice). The new code relies on the defer to clean up after each call, so the next call starts clean. This is fine, but on the very first call s.stack is nil and len 0 — worth confirming clear(nil) is a no-op (it is in Go 1.21+) and noting the lifecycle in a comment.

issues.description: No test exhibited for the reported state-reuse bug; proofs of correctness should be backed by a regression test.
issues.detail: The PR description says it "fixes non-zero elements in the stack slice" and "fixes cleanup by clearing state on completion," but the diff shows no accompanying test. Per the discipline: beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it. Add a test that calls Sort twice on the same Sorter and asserts identical output.

review.summary: The change is a small, sensible simplification: collapse a redundant state, and move state/stack cleanup to a defer so a Sorter is reusable across Sort() calls. The algorithmic core (DFS-as-loop with post-visit emission) is unchanged, and the fix to emit-then-mark-sorted ordering inside the yield branch is correct. My concerns are literate-programming concerns: the loop invariant and state semantics are not written down, the comment has fresh typos, and there is no regression test for the reuse bug this PR claims to fix. UNDER-AUDITED rather than wrong — RIGOROUS once invariant comment and a reuse test are added.
